chinese_source: Yijing, Nanhai jigui neifa zhuan (sent to China 691)

chinese_source: Yijing, Nanhai jigui neifa zhuan, grammar chapter (sent to China 691)
event: Yijing names Bhartrhari's works, makes him a contemporary of Dharmapala, and states 'it is forty years since his death' - implying death c. 651-652 CE
firmness_reason: Firm as a record of what Yijing reports; Probable as history (Frauwallner-line pushback and the two-Bhartrhari escape hatch are documented in the spine)

chinese_source: Jiu Tang shu / Xin Tang shu, Tianzhu accounts
event: Harsha ('king of Magadha') sends an embassy to Taizong; the Tang reply mission under Li Yibiao with Wang Xuance is in India 643-645; Xuanzang received at Harsha's court, Kannauj assembly 643
firmness_reason: Court annal record of received embassies, reign-era dated at every step
notes: Cf. spine C19/C21.

chinese_source: Xin Tang shu, Western Regions (Kashmir entry)
event: Embassy from Candrapida of Kashmir reaches Xuanzong's court requesting aid against the Arabs and Tibet
firmness_reason: Annalistic record of a received embassy; the name equation Zhentuoluobili = Candrapida is standard
notes: Campaign case 9: Kalhana's received chronology has Candrapida dead by 688 - the annals put him on the throne in 713.
references: Xin Tang shu, Kashmir entry; Stein, Rajatarangini introduction; Campaign CORRECTIONS.md case 9

chinese_source: Xin Tang shu / Tang edicts (Kashmir entry)
event: Tang court invests Candrapida by edict as King of Kashmir (720); a further edict (722) praises Kashmir for provisioning Tang troops in Gilgit
firmness_reason: Court edicts recorded in the annals with reign-era dates
notes: Cunningham's computation: by this investiture Kalhana's chronology is in error by exactly 31 years for Candrapida.
references: Xin Tang shu, Kashmir entry; Cunningham, Ancient Geography / Rajatarangini chronology discussions; Campaign CORRECTIONS.md case 9

chinese_source: Xin Tang shu, Western Regions (Kashmir entry)
event: Muduobi (Muktapida), Candrapida's younger brother, sends the envoy Wuliduo requesting investiture, offering troops and a temple by the Mahapadma lake; invested by the Tang court
date_raw: Xuanzong reign; Stein dates the embassy after the Baltistan operations of 736-747

notes: Campaign case 9: corrected placement Lalitaditya c. 724/725-760/761, against Kalhana-derived 699-736.

chinese_source: Jiu Tang shu (Old Book of Tang), Nepal (Nipoluo) account; Old Tibetan Annals frame
event: After the usurpation by his uncle Visnugupta, Narendradeva flees to Tibet; the Tibetans re-establish him on the Nepalese throne (641), making Nepal a Tibetan client; Nepal supplies 7,000 troops to Wang Xuance's 648 campaign and the Tangshu describes Narendradeva as reigning king in information current to c. 648
date_raw: Restoration pegged to 641 (Zhenguan 15 era frame; Tibetan annals place the Nepal intervention in the early 640s)
firmness_reason: Event sequence is annalistic and the Tibetan record concurs; the exact year 641 is the standard scholarly peg within 641-643 rather than a year stated in so many words, and the Tangshu narrative compresses the inscriptional Jishnugupta/Dhruvadeva tangle
notes: Campaign case 10 verdict CORRECTED: the vaimsavali chronology supplies no absolute date for this segment; the Tang/Tibetan peg is the only one.
references: Jiu Tang shu, Nepal account; Old Tibetan Annals; Campaign CORRECTIONS.md case 10

indian_entity: Huna king of Gandhara (Song Yun's audience)
chinese_source: Song Yun's itinerary, preserved in Luoyang qielan ji (c. 547)
event: Song Yun (embassy 518-522) meets the Huna king ruling Gandhara - cruel, unbelieving, on campaign - whose people conquered Gandhara two generations earlier; the Kaniska stupa still stands
date_raw: Northern Wei, Shengui 1 to Zhengguang 3 (518-522); audience c. 520
firmness_reason: Dated eyewitness observation; the king is unnamed and the Mihirakula identification, though standard, is an inference
notes: Campaign case 11 verdict CORROBORATED: 520 falls inside Mihirakula's epigraphic floruit (c. 515-542); 'two generations since the conquest' gives a conquest horizon c. 460-490. Cf. spine C14.
references: Luoyang qielan ji (Song Yun itinerary); Campaign CORRECTIONS.md case 11

chinese_source: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu ji (646)
event: Xuanzang narrates Mihirakula's persecution and his defeat/capture by the Gupta king Baladitya, but places him 'several hundred years' before his own time - the actual gap is c. 100 years
firmness_reason: The narrative corroborates the Baladitya-defeat tradition, but the stated interval is a demonstrable Chinese-side error (c. 100 years reported as several hundred); carried as a reliability flag, not a bound
notes: Campaign case 11: the campaign's clearest proof that pilgrim-reported intervals are tradition, while pilgrim observation is record.
references: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu ji; Campaign CORRECTIONS.md case 11

chinese_source: Faxian, Foguo ji (Record of Buddhist Kingdoms)
event: Faxian in India 399-414 (three years at Pataliputra): a prosperous, lightly governed paramount kingdom centred at Pataliputra; the king is never named
firmness_reason: Itinerary is internally dated and firm; the identification of the unnamed king's frame with Candragupta II (r. c. 375-415, inscriptions to Gupta year 93 = 412) is inferential
notes: Campaign case 12 (corroboration test) verdict CORROBORATED: the frame holds; graded Probable because an unnamed king's prosperity would corroborate a wrong reign almost as smoothly. Cf. spine C11.
references: Faxian, Foguo ji (trans. Legge 1886); Campaign CORRECTIONS.md case 12

chinese_source: Song annals (Song Shi / Song Huiyao), Zhulian (Chola) file
event: First Chola mission reaches the Song court; the sending king is named Lo-ts'a-lo-ts'a (Rajaraja). Dispatched in Rajaraja's name one to two sailing seasons earlier; he died in 1014, months before the arrival
firmness_reason: Annalistic entry with reign-era date; name equation phonetically transparent
notes: Campaign case 13 verdict CORROBORATED. The Song file also preserves Srivijaya's earlier misrepresentation of Chola as its dependency, which this mission corrected at court.
references: Song Shi, Zhulian account; Campaign CORRECTIONS.md case 13

chinese_source: Song annals, Zhulian (Chola) file
event: Chola mission from Shi-lo-cha Yin-to-lo Chu-lo (Sri Raja Indra Chola = Rajendra I) reaches the Song court
firmness_reason: Annalistic entry with reign-era date; name equation transparent
notes: Falls inside Rajendra's inscriptionally dated sole reign (1014-1044): exact corroboration.
references: Song Shi, Zhulian account; Campaign CORRECTIONS.md case 13

chinese_source: Song annals, Zhulian (Chola) file
event: Mission of seventy merchants from Ti-hua-kia-lo (Deva Kulottunga = Kulottunga I) received at the Song court; 81,800 strings of copper cash given for its tribute goods
firmness_reason: Annalistic entry with reign-era date; name equation standard
notes: Independently confirms Kulottunga I (accession 1070 by the inscriptional computation) on the throne in 1077.
references: Song Shi, Zhulian account; Campaign CORRECTIONS.md case 13

indian_entity: Srivijaya (Fo-shih) as a Buddhist learning centre
chinese_source: Yijing, travel memoir and Nanhai jigui neifa zhuan
event: Yijing spends six months in Fo-shih (Srivijaya) in 671: a fortified royal city with more than a thousand monks, learning ranked with Madhyadesa's; he studies Sanskrit grammar there and recommends it to Chinese students
firmness_reason: Dated eyewitness observation - the spine's zero-lag class
notes: Campaign case 14 verdict BOUNDED: a mature Srivijaya existed in 671, eleven years before its first surviving inscription (Kedukan Bukit, 682); the rise is bounded to the 660s at the latest.
references: Yijing, Nanhai jigui / memoir (trans. Takakusu); Campaign CORRECTIONS.md case 14

chinese_source: Yijing, travel memoir
event: Yijing passed Mo-lo-yu (Malayu) as a separate country in 673; by his return stay in Srivijaya (685-689) he records that Mo-lo-yu 'has become Fo-shih'
firmness_reason: Two dated eyewitness observations bracketing the event
notes: Annexation of Malayu bracketed to (673, 689] - Srivijaya's first datable act of expansion.
references: Yijing, memoir; Campaign CORRECTIONS.md case 14

chinese_source: Baolin Zhuan (801), lost; known through quotation and the list it standardised
event: The Baolin Zhuan fixes the canonical list of 28 Indian patriarchs ending Prajnatara (27) - Bodhidharma (28), reopening the line the Fu Fazang Yinyuan Zhuan (472) had closed at Simha's beheading by inserting Basiasita, Punyamitra and Prajnatara
firmness_reason: The fixing of the list at 801 is the standard scholarly account, but the text is lost and the list is known through later quotation
notes: First attestation of Prajnatara in any source. The names between Simha and Bodhidharma are the least stable segment across competing Tang lists (Lidai Fabao Ji c. 775 differs).
references: Encyclopedia of Buddhism, 'Lineage' entry; Bodhidharma Case 16 build, BODHIDHARMA.md section 4

chinese_source: Luoyang Qielan Ji notice (547); Xu Gaoseng Zhuan biography (645-667)
event: Bodhidharma's defensible floruit: present in Luoyang 516-526, dead before 534; arrival best supported under the Liu Song (by the 470s) per Daoxuan
firmness_reason: Two independent near-contemporary witnesses; the window rests on the Yongning Temple inference and Daoxuan's pre-534 death horizon
notes: Refines and bounds the contested seed record bodhidharma-arrival-c520: the 520/527 arrival dates are later traditional assignments; 527 is falsified by this window.
references: Yang Xuanzhi, Luoyang Qielan Ji; Daoxuan, Xu Gaoseng Zhuan, T.2060; Bodhidharma Case 16 build, BODHIDHARMA.md sections 1-2

chinese_source: Near-contemporary biographical records; East Mountain community tradition
event: Floruit of Daoxin (580-651), fourth Chinese node of the Lengjia chart
firmness_reason: Attested in near-contemporary records; dates conventional in the biographical tradition and consistent with the Hongren succession
notes: Daoxin (b. 580) to Hongren (b. 601) is the first normal generational interval (~21 years) in the chart.
references: Bodhidharma Case 16 build, BODHIDHARMA.md section 2

chinese_source: Epitaph for Faru (638-689), dated inscription
event: The epitaph for Faru gives the first lineage succession of any kind: Bodhidharma - Huike - Sengcan - Daoxin - Hongren - Faru. Before 689 no source arranges these men as a succession
firmness_reason: A dated inscription; the lineage claim's first appearance is fixed by the stone's own date
notes: TAQ on the lineage idea itself: the chart is a late-7th-century artefact, ~160 years after Bodhidharma's death.
references: Faru epitaph (689); McRae, Seeing Through Zen (2003)

chinese_source: Gaoseng Zhuan / Xu Gaoseng Zhuan biographical tradition and translation catalogues
event: Death of Gunabhadra (394-468), the Lankavatara translator — the terminus that constrains the Lengjia Shizi Ji chart: any personal discipleship of Bodhidharma under Gunabhadra must end by 468
firmness_reason: Death year from the dated biographical tradition for a translator whose activity (435 arrival, 443 Lankavatara) is catalogue-anchored; not itself a dated colophon
notes: Chart constraint, not a text TAQ: with the 527-arrival tradition it forces a >=59-year gap between discipleship and arrival; with the Liu Song arrival (<=479) it forces arrival by the 460s.
references: Xu Gaoseng Zhuan biography of Gunabhadra; Bodhidharma Case 16 build, BODHIDHARMA.md section 2

chinese_source: Multiple biographical notices; Faru epitaph (689) from inside his community
event: Floruit of Hongren (601-674; some sources 602-675), fifth Chinese node of the Lengjia chart
firmness_reason: Multiple independent attestations plus a dated inscription (689) by his disciple's circle; the first node after Gunabhadra where cross-dating fully works
notes: Some sources give 602-675; the one-year variance is recorded rather than resolved.
references: Faru epitaph (689); Bodhidharma Case 16 build, BODHIDHARMA.md section 2

chinese_source: Xu Gaoseng Zhuan biography of Huike; later biographical tradition
event: Death of Huike (487-593), Bodhidharma's disciple and recipient of the 4-fascicle Lankavatara per Daoxuan
firmness_reason: Death era consistent across the biographical tradition; the implied 107-year lifespan (487-593) is longevity inflation and is not load-bearing
notes: Chart node 2 of the Lengjia line. Daoxuan has his arm lost to bandits; the self-severing version is first epigraphically attested on a stele of 798.
references: Daoxuan, Xu Gaoseng Zhuan, T.2060; Shahar, The Shaolin Monastery (2008)

chinese_source: Baolin Zhuan (801) patriarch list; first extant narratives Zutang Ji (952) and Jingde Chuandeng Lu (1004)
event: First attestation of Prajnatara, Bodhidharma's putative teacher and 27th Indian patriarch: an ATTESTATION record, not a date for a life. No attestation exists in Tanlin, Daoxuan, the Lengjia Shizi Ji, the Fu Fazang list (472), or any Indian, Tibetan, Central Asian or non-Chan Chinese source
firmness_reason: The figure is attested only inside Chan lineage literature and only from 801, ~270 years after Bodhidharma's death; graded contested as a person, firm as an attestation date
notes: Default verdict of the Case 16 build: a lineage construction at the seam where the Fu Fazang list had declared the transmission extinct. A mid-9th-c. Nalanda namesake (folios preserved in Japan via Enchin) is unconnected. The female identification is a modern conjecture (Benson 2008).
references: Bodhidharma Case 16 build, BODHIDHARMA.md section 4

chinese_source: Later Chan biographical tradition
event: Traditional death year of Sengcan, third node of the Lengjia chart after Bodhidharma and Huike
firmness_reason: Almost no independent attestation; the Huike-Sengcan link itself is flagged as tenuous in the scholarship (Whalen Lai). Carried with the grade shown, not dropped
notes: The chart's weakest node: a death year with no documented life. His 606 death, 13 years after Huike's, creates the downstream generational squeeze analysed in the Case 16 build.
references: Bodhidharma Case 16 build, BODHIDHARMA.md section 2

chinese_source: Yang Xuanzhi, Luoyang Qielan Ji (547)
event: Yongning Temple built 516 and destroyed by fire 534; Yang Xuanzhi's notice places Bodhidharma admiring its stupa in the intact temple, bounding his Luoyang presence to 516-526 on Broughton's reading
firmness_reason: Temple construction/destruction are court-record dates; the sighting window is an inference from the gazetteer's description of the intact temple
notes: The hardest single terminus in the Bodhidharma dossier: falsifies the 527 Liang-arrival tradition, which postdates this entire window.
references: Yang Xuanzhi, Luoyang Qielan Ji; Broughton, The Bodhidharma Anthology (1999)

chinese_source: Duarte Barbosa, The Book of Duarte Barbosa (composed c. 1516-1518) — first written record of the legend
event: Barbosa records that a Malabar king ('Chirimay Perumal') was converted by Moorish traders, sailed to Mecca and died there or en route, his kingdom partitioned — and dates the event 'more than 600 years before our time', i.e. c. 900 CE. No Prophet, no moon-splitting, no Malik ibn Dinar
firmness_reason: The legend existed in oral circulation by c. 1516 (firm); the composition window of Barbosa's book is approximate, hence probable for the record as dated
notes: TAQ for the LEGEND, and a synchronism against its modern form: the earliest witness dates the conversion to c. 900 and knows nothing of the 629 CE / Prophet's-lifetime synchronism, which is a later layer.
references: Barbosa, The Book of Duarte Barbosa (c. 1516-1518); More, J. B. P., on the Portuguese notices of the legend

indian_entity: Cheraman Perumal conversion legend (full Malik ibn Dinar cycle)
chinese_source: Zainuddin Makhdum II, Tuhfat al-Mujahidin (Arabic, completed c. 1583) — first full devotional telling
event: The full cycle exists in writing: the pilgrims en route to Adam's Foot, the moon-splitting narration, the king's secret departure and death abroad, his letters, and Malik ibn Dinar's party founding mosques at Kodungallur and the named ports. Zainuddin himself dates the conversion to two hundred years after the Prophet (c. 820s), NOT to the Prophet's lifetime
firmness_reason: Dated, extant, authored text — the standard first history of Kerala by a Keralite
notes: TAQ for the developed legend. Its internal dating (c. 820s) is the legend's own earliest full-text chronology and contradicts the 629 CE date now displayed at the mosque.
references: Zainuddin Makhdum II, Tuhfat al-Mujahidin (c. 1583), trans. Nainar (1942); More, J. B. P., on the Tuhfat's dating of the conversion

chinese_source: Ibn Battuta, Rihla — eyewitness account of his Malabar sojourn, 1342-1347
event: Describes mosques in every Malabar port town, named qadis at Calicut and Kollam, the cathedral mosque at Hili (Ezhimala) enriched by sailors' vows, and a Muslim shah bandar governing Calicut's port — Malabar Islam as a long-established institution
firmness_reason: Dated eyewitness travel account, internally consistent with the 14th-century mosque epigraphy of Kozhikode (Kuttichira)
notes: Terminus: Malabar mosques are FIRM by the 1340s. Battuta records no foundation legend for Kodungallur and no 629 tradition.
references: Ibn Battuta, Rihla, Gibb translation, Malabar chapters

indian_entity: Joseph Rabban and the Jewish guild (Anjuvannam) of Kodungallur
chinese_source: Jewish copper plates of Cochin — Old Malayalam (Vattezhuthu with Grantha) royal charter of Bhaskara Ravi Varma (local epigraphy)
event: Bhaskara Ravi grants Joseph Rabban the rights of the Anjuvannam merchant guild and aristocratic privileges at Muyirikkottu (Kodungallur) — a chartered Jewish merchant lordship at the old Chera capital
date_raw: 38th regnal year of Bhaskara Ravi Varma
firmness_reason: Epigraphic consensus (Narayanan 1972 and successors) dates the plates c. 1000 CE via Bhaskara Ravi's accession c. 962; the community's traditional date is 379 CE
notes: Web anchor for the Kodungallur node: the plates are genuine, their traditional date overshoots the epigraphic date by ~620 years — the same tradition-vs-attestation gap shape as the Cheraman mosque claim (629 vs 11th-12th-c. fabric). Jewish presence on the coast is independently firm by 849 (Hebrew signatures on the Quilon plates).
references: Narayanan, M. G. S., Cultural Symbiosis in Kerala (1972); Perumals of Kerala (1996/2013)

chinese_source: Arabic foundation inscription (copper slab) preserved in the Madayi Mosque (local epigraphy as reported in the Kerala survey literature)
event: Foundation inscription dates the Madayi Mosque to Hijra 518 — the earliest dated mosque-foundation inscription in Kerala
firmness_reason: Reported consistently across the survey literature; no modern epigraphic edition was available to the build
notes: Mosque foundations on the Malabar coast become epigraphically visible in the 12th century. The date 1124 is sometimes misattributed in polemical literature to the Kodungallur (Cheraman) mosque, which has no dated foundation inscription.
references: Malabar Muslims / Mappila survey literature on the Madayi inscription

indian_entity: Settled Muslim community on India's west coast (Saymur/Chaul)
chinese_source: Al-Masudi, Muruj al-Dhahab (completed 943, revised 956), reporting his Indian sojourn of c. 915-916
event: Masudi reports some 10,000 bayasira (locally born Muslims) at Saymur (Chaul, Konkan coast) with ordinary and Friday mosques, protected by the Hindu king — a settled, second-generation, mosque-building Muslim community under Hindu rule
firmness_reason: Eyewitness-grade traveller report, but the named town is Saymur on the Konkan coast, NOT Malabar proper; the figure of 10,000 is a traveller's round number
notes: Bounds the regional pattern: by c. 915 mosque-building Muslim settlement under Hindu kings is normal on the west coast north of Malabar. It does not attest Malabar itself, and Masudi tells no convert-king story.
references: Al-Masudi, Muruj al-Dhahab wa Ma'adin al-Jawahir (943/956)

indian_entity: Muslim burial at Panthalayani Kollam, Malabar Coast
chinese_source: Arabic tombstone inscription outside the Juma mosque, Panthalayani Kollam (local epigraphy as reported in the Kerala survey literature)
event: Tombstone records the death of a Muslim (ibn Udthorman) in Hijra 166 — a Muslim buried on the Malabar coast, implying a burying community
firmness_reason: Reading circulates through secondary survey literature, not a modern epigraphic edition; AH 166 = 782-783 CE (repeatedly misprinted as '752 CE' in the secondary literature — a conversion error)
notes: If the reading holds, this is the earliest dated Muslim presence on the coast, two-thirds of a century before the Quilon plates. Grade is explicitly hostage to a critical re-edition of the stone.
references: Malabar Muslims / Mappila survey literature on the Panthalayani tombstone; Heritage: Journal of Multidisciplinary Studies in Archaeology 8.1 (2020) — prints the erroneous '752 CE' conversion

indian_entity: Muslim community of Kollam (Quilon), Malabar Coast
chinese_source: Quilon (Tarisapalli) copper plates — Chera royal charter of Ayyan Adikal under Sthanu Ravi Kulasekhara, witness plate (local epigraphy; the correlation source here is epigraphic, not Chinese)
event: Eleven Muslim witnesses sign, in Kufic Arabic, a royal charter granting privileges to the Christian Tarisapalli church at Kollam, alongside witnesses signing in Pahlavi and Hebrew — a settled Muslim community of charter-witnessing standing exists at Kollam
date_raw: 5th regnal year of Sthanu Ravi Kulasekhara (Kollam era 24/25)
firmness_reason: Dated royal charter, extant plates; the standard epigraphic dating of the Tarisapalli grant
notes: Earliest FIRM attestation of a Muslim community on the Malabar coast. The signatures attest a community, not a mosque building; no mosque at Kollam or Kodungallur is dated by this document.
references: Quilon Syrian copper plates (849 CE), plate 5 witness signatures; Narayanan, M. G. S., Perumals of Kerala (1996/2013)

indian_entity: Kollam (Kulam Mali) in the Arab-Chinese sea trade
chinese_source: Akhbar al-Sin wa'l-Hind (Accounts of China and India), compiled 851, attributed to the merchant Sulaiman — an Arabic witness to the China run, held in the spine as the traveller-record class
event: Describes the working route Siraf-Muscat-Kulam Mali (Kollam), with Chinese ships paying heavy port dues at Kollam — Arab shipping serves Malabar as a mature entrepot system
firmness_reason: Dated compilation; the itinerary is first-hand merchant reporting
notes: Attests Arab TRADE presence and Kollam's role. It does NOT mention a Muslim community, a mosque, or a convert king in Malabar — a registered negative for the Cheraman claim.
references: Akhbar al-Sin wa'l-Hind (851), Ferrand (1922) / Mackintosh-Smith (2014) editions

indian_entity: Alopen's mission — first documented Church of the East arrival in China
chinese_source: Xi'an Stele (781), corroborated in outline by Tang Huiyao fasc. 49
event: Alopen arrives at Chang'an from Daqin carrying scriptures and images; received by Fang Xuanling; the scriptures are translated in the imperial library
firmness_reason: Retrospective by 146 years on the stele; no contemporary Tang document records the arrival itself, though the 638 edict and the church's Tang presence are independently recorded
notes: Dates the ARRIVAL of the Church of the East in China — a transmission event. It attests the institution that carried the Thomas tradition east; it is not evidence about Thomas (1st c.).
references: Xi'an Stele inscription (781); Tang Huiyao fasc. 49 (compiled 961)

indian_entity: Gondophares I, Indo-Parthian king (the 'Gudnaphar' of the Acts of Thomas)
chinese_source: Takht-i-Bahi Kharoshthi inscription (NON-CHINESE external anchor; this field carries the dating record per schema)
event: Inscription dated in era year 103 and in Gondophares' 26th regnal year. On the standard identification of the unnamed era with the Azes era (= Vikrama era, year 1 = 57 BCE), year 103 = 46 CE and accession falls c. 20 CE
date_raw: Era year 103, regnal year 26 (era unnamed in the inscription)
firmness_reason: The inscription is contemporary and names the king, but the absolute year rests entirely on identifying its unnamed era with Azes/Vikrama — Bivar (Encyclopaedia Iranica) treats the identification as settled; Robert Senior's alternative chronology reassigns the inscription to a later Gondophares
notes: Load-bearing anchor for the Acts of Thomas' Gondophares (reign c. 20-46 CE on the standard reading). Caveats: 'Gondophares' later became a dynastic title (Gondophares IV Sases, mid-to-late 1st c.), so the name alone does not fix which bearer an undated text means; his brother Gad in the Acts matches Gadana/Gad among the subordinate names on his coinage. Proposed as a non-Chinese external anchor, on the same logic as the Aihole prasasti in the BU benchmark panel.
references: Bivar, 'Gondophares', Encyclopaedia Iranica XI (2002); Senior, 'More Gondophares, Less Azes', Oriental Numismatic Society Occasional Paper 25 (1991)

indian_entity: Jingjiao community at Luoyang (Daqin Jingjiao Xuanyuan Zhiben Jing pillar)
chinese_source: Luoyang Jingjiao pillar inscription (recovered at Luoyang, published from 2006)
event: Stone pillar erected at Luoyang carrying the Xuanyuan Zhiben Jing text with a Syriac inscription naming East Syriac clergy — a second dated Jingjiao monument after the Xi'an Stele
firmness_reason: Self-dated pillar; recovered and published only in 2006, so the specialist literature is younger than for the Xi'an Stele
notes: The closest thing to a dated Jingjiao colophon-monument after 781. Its text is doctrinal (Xuanyuan Zhiben Jing); no Thomas material.
references: Luoyang pillar inscription (814/815); Saeki, The Nestorian Documents and Relics in China (1937), for the text's Dunhuang witness

indian_entity: Tarisapalli church, Kollam (Quilon) — East Syriac-linked Christian community in Kerala
chinese_source: Quilon (Tarisapalli) copper plates (NON-CHINESE external anchor; this field carries the dating record per schema)
event: Ayyan Adikal, chief of Kollam, grants land and privileges to the Tarisapalli church under the Persian merchant Maruvan Sapir Iso; the witness plate carries signatures in Pahlavi, Kufic Arabic and Judeo-Persian
date_raw: 5th regnal year of the Chera king Sthanu Ravi Kulasekhara
firmness_reason: Dated by the regnal year of an epigraphically anchored Chera king; the plates survive; the Pahlavi witness signatures were edited by Cereti (2009)
notes: Proves a chartered, Persian-linked Christian church on the Malabar coast by 849 — and nothing about its founder. Community tradition associates the migration behind the grant with Mar Sabor and Mar Proth (arrival c. 825), but the plates name Maruvan Sapir Iso; the identification is traditional, not epigraphic.
references: Cereti, 'The Pahlavi Signatures on the Quilon Copper Plates' (2009); Varier & Veluthat, Tarissappallippattayam (2013)

indian_entity: Imperial authorisation of Jingjiao in Tang China
chinese_source: Edict text preserved in Tang Huiyao fasc. 49 (compiled 961) and quoted on the Xi'an Stele (781)
event: Emperor Taizong's edict approves propagation of the Daqin (Jingjiao) religion and authorises a temple in the Yining ward of Chang'an with twenty-one monks
firmness_reason: Edict text survives in a Song-compiled Tang institutional history and on the 781 stele; two carriers, neither contemporary paper
notes: The earliest Chinese state document on Christianity. It names the religion and its Daqin origin; it does not name Thomas or any apostle.
references: Tang Huiyao fasc. 49; Xi'an Stele inscription (781)

indian_entity: Official status of Jingjiao temples in Tang China
chinese_source: Edict of Tianbao 4, preserved in Tang Huiyao / Tang institutional records
event: Imperial edict renames the religion's temples from Bosi si ('Persian temples') to Daqin si ('Daqin temples') in the two capitals and all prefectures, on the stated ground that the religion originates in Daqin, not Persia
firmness_reason: Edict text preserved in Tang institutional compilations; consistent with the stele's account of the church's status
notes: Institutional anchor only: it fixes the church's recognised presence empire-wide in 745. No Thomas content.
references: Tang Huiyao fasc. 49; Saeki, The Nestorian Documents and Relics in China (1937)

indian_entity: Church of the East (Jingjiao) mission in China — the eastern carrier of the Thomas tradition
chinese_source: Xi'an (Daqin Jingjiao) Stele, erected at the Daqin temple, Chang'an; composed by Jingjing (Adam)
event: Stele erected, recording the Jingjiao church's history in China from 635 to 781 and naming its clergy in Chinese and Syriac (~70 Syriac names; Catholicos Hnanisho' named)
firmness_reason: Self-dated inscription; the stone survives (unearthed 1623-1625)
notes: The stele does NOT name Thomas anywhere. It dates the institution's China history (635-781), not the apostle. The arriving church traced its own apostolic origin to Thomas in its Syriac tradition, but that self-understanding is not a Chinese record of Thomas.
references: Saeki, The Nestorian Documents and Relics in China (1937); Nicolini-Zani, Christian Monks on Chinese Soil (2006)

chinese_source: EXTERNAL epigraphic anchor (non-Chinese): Nalanda copper plate of Devapala, regnal year 39, found 1921 in the antechamber of Monastery 1, Nalanda (Epigraphia Indica XVII)
event: At the request of Balaputradeva, Sailendra king of Suvarnadvipa (Srivijaya), who has built a monastery at Nalanda, Devapala grants five named villages for its monks' requisites, the copying of texts, and the upkeep of the vihara
firmness_reason: A dated royal charter excavated in situ at Nalanda itself; the only uncertainty is Devapala's accession year (c. 810-821 in competing chronologies), which sets the 849-861 window
notes: Endowment rate: five villages for ONE vihara (~30-60 residents) implies roughly 6-12 monks supported per village — the same order as Yijing's implied 15 per village, and a cross-check against Huili's implied 100 per village. Also a Srivijaya synchronism: Balaputradeva's reign must intersect this window.
references: N. G. Majumdar, Epigraphia Indica XVII, The Nalanda Copper-plate of Devapaladeva; Varendra Research Society Monograph no. 1 (1926)

chinese_source: EXTERNAL pilgrim anchor (Tibetan, non-Chinese): Biography of Dharmasvamin (Chag lo-tsa-ba Chos-rje-dpal), dictated by the pilgrim, tr. Roerich (1959)
event: Dharmasvamin studies at Nalanda in 1235 for about six months: the site is damaged and largely deserted after the Turushka raids, but two viharas remain serviceable and the aged abbot Rahulasribhadra (over 90) is still teaching a class of about 70 students
date_raw: Visit dated by the biography's itinerary to 1235 (in India 1234-1236)
firmness_reason: Near-eyewitness (dictated by the pilgrim to his biographer); the small numbers are non-round and circumstantial (70 students, a named teacher, a dated raid scare) — the most credible population data point in the whole series, at the series' end
notes: His hearsay memory of Nalanda's former extent — 7 temples, 14 large and 84 small monasteries — is graded rhetoric in the stats file (84 is a canonical number), but the 70 students is a count, not a trope. Refutes the textbook claim of total destruction c. 1193-1200: the institution was wounded, not annihilated, and teaching continued four decades on.
references: George Roerich (tr.), Biography of Dharmasvamin (1959), with A. S. Altekar's introduction; Biography of Dharmasvamin, Tibetan text ed. Roerich

chinese_source: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji (646) and Huili, Life of Xuanzang — attribution of the founding vihara to King Shakraditya; corroborated on the ground by Gupta royal clay sealings excavated in Monastery 1, Nalanda (EXTERNAL epigraphic anchor, non-Chinese)
event: Nalanda's first royal vihara is founded under Kumaragupta I (Xuanzang's Shakraditya); clay sealings of the Gupta royal line and of the Nalanda sangha were excavated in Monastery 1, physically anchoring the foundation tradition in the Gupta period
firmness_reason: Shakraditya = Kumaragupta I is an identification, not a naming in any inscription; but the excavated Gupta sealings put royal Gupta patronage on the site in exactly this window
notes: Xuanzang's own chronology for Shakraditya ('not long after the Buddha's nirvana') is worthless; the identification rests on the sealings and the six-king building sequence in Huili. Conventional founding date c. 427 CE falls inside this reign window. Faxian (c. 410) saw only a village and stupa at Nalanda — a negative attestation just before the window opens.
references: Beal, Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), Nalanda chapter; Hirananda Sastri, Nalanda and its Epigraphic Material (1942); ASI excavation record, Monastery 1 sealings

chinese_source: EXTERNAL epigraphic anchor (non-Chinese): Ghosrawa (Ghosrawan) stone inscription, time of Devapala (Indian Antiquary XVII, 1888)
event: Viradeva of Nagarahara — trained at the Kaniska vihara near Peshawar, resident at Yasovarmanapura vihara — is elected by the sangha, under Devapala's patronage, to preside over the monasteries of Nalanda, and builds a vihara and chaityas at Ghosrawa
date_raw: Undated; reign of Devapala, palaeography late 9th century (Fleet)
firmness_reason: Undated inscription; the window is Devapala's reign widened by Fleet's palaeographic judgement (latter half of the 9th century). Content — a royally backed abbatial appointment — is not in doubt
notes: Governance anchor: in the later 9th century Nalanda still has a sangha that elects its head and a Pala king who backs the appointment. No population figure.
references: J. F. Fleet, Indian Antiquary XVII (1888), Ghosrawa Buddhist Inscription; Bhagwant Sahai, The Inscriptions of Bihar (1983)

chinese_source: Huili (completed by Yancong), Life of Xuanzang (Da Ci'en Si Sanzang Fashi Zhuan), presented c. 688
event: Huili's biography states that Nalanda's residents and visitors together 'always reach 10,000', with about 100 lecture pulpits daily, 1,000 men able to explain twenty collections, 500 able to explain thirty, and Harsa's endowment of about 100 villages with 200 supplying householders each
firmness_reason: This record anchors the CLAIM's first carrier, not the population: the figure is a disciple's panegyric, is ~3x both Xuanzang's own text and Yijing's eyewitness count, and exceeds the excavated residential plant's capacity by 5-15x (see nalanda/NALANDA-STATS.md capacity test)
notes: Modern '1,500 faculty' is a sum of Huili's 1,000 + 500 mastery tiers; '2,000 teachers' has no pre-modern carrier at all. Huili's architectural data (eight halls) agree with Yijing exactly — the inflation is specific to crowds, not buildings.
references: Beal, The Life of Hiuen-Tsiang (1911), Nalanda description; Li Rongxi, The Life of Xuanzang (1995)

chinese_source: Hyecho (Silla), Wang Ocheonchukguk Jeon (Memoir of the Pilgrimage to the Five Kingdoms of India), Dunhuang manuscript
event: The Korean pilgrim Hyecho passes through Magadha in 723-728 and names Nalanda among its living monasteries; he gives no population figure — a dated presence attestation between Yijing and the Yasovarman inscription
firmness_reason: Eyewitness itinerary, but the surviving Dunhuang scroll is fragmentary (first volume and end of third lost) and his Nalanda notice is brief; value is chronological, not statistical
notes: Negative-statistical value: the one 8th-century pilgrim who might have updated the population series gives no number, so the series jumps from Yijing (685) to epigraphy.
references: Yang Han-sung et al., The Hye Ch'o Diary (1984); Dunhuang manuscript P.3532, Bibliotheque nationale de France

chinese_source: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji (compiled 646), Nalanda chapter
event: Xuanzang resides at Nalanda under abbot Silabhadra; his own Records put the resident priests at 'several thousand', describe eight halls inside one brick wall, and give the gatekeeper's failure rate for would-be debaters as seven or eight in ten
firmness_reason: Eyewitness resident, but his population figure is an uncounted round phrase ('several thousand'); his architectural count (eight halls) is corroborated independently by Yijing
notes: The famous 10,000 figure is NOT in this text — it is in Huili's biography (see nalanda-huili-ten-thousand-claim). Xuanzang's own number is consistent with Yijing's 3,000+ a generation later.
references: Beal, Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884), vol. II, Nalanda chapter; Da Tang Xiyu Ji, fascicle IX

chinese_source: EXTERNAL epigraphic anchor (non-Chinese): Nalanda stone inscription of the reign of Yasovarman of Kanauj, found in the southern verandah debris of Monastery 1 (Epigraphia Indica XX, no. 2)
event: Malada, son of Yasovarman's minister Tikina ('Lord of the North'), makes a permanent endowment (aksaya-nivi) to Baladitya's temple at Nalanda funding daily distribution of rice, curds and ghee to the monks — the mahavihara is endowed and feeding a resident sangha under Kanauj's king
date_raw: Reign of Yasovarman of Kanauj; the date as read ('731' of an unspecified era) does not convert cleanly
firmness_reason: The inscription is physically in situ at Nalanda and its content is unambiguous; only its era attribution is disputed, so the window is Yasovarman's reign rather than a single year
notes: No head-count is given — a provisions anchor, not a population one. The donor's father bears the Turkic title Tikina (tegin), a nice datum for Nalanda's Central Asian connections in the 8th century.
references: Hirananda Sastri, Epigraphia Indica XX (1929-30), pp. 37-46; Bhagwant Sahai, The Inscriptions of Bihar (1983)

chinese_source: Yijing, Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan (Record of Buddhist Practices, sent home 691) and his Memoir of eminent monks
event: Yijing resides ten years at Nalanda and reports, as an administrator of monastic routine: more than 3,000 resident monks (Memoir: 3,500), eight halls, more than 300 apartments, and landed endowment of more than 200 villages accumulated from successive kings
date_raw: Tang, Xianheng to Chuigong eras; residence 673-685, Record sent home Tianshou 2 (691)
firmness_reason: Eyewitness with an administrative (not panegyric) register; his 300 apartments match the excavated ground-floor cell estimate (~250-320) and his 15 monks-per-village ratio is internally consistent with the Devapala plate's endowment rate — the dataset's anchor population witness
notes: Some manuscripts of the Record read 5,000 for the resident count; Takakusu judged 3,000 the correct reading. Even 3,000 exceeds the excavated core's design capacity (~450-650 cells), so his figure implies the unexcavated remainder of the walled complex and/or shared occupancy — see the capacity test.
references: Takakusu, A Record of the Buddhist Religion as Practised in India and the Malay Archipelago (1896); Yijing, Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan, T.2125

chinese_source: Ayuwang zhuan (T.2042), translated by An Faqin (fl. 281-306); re-translated as Ayuwang jing (T.2043) by Sanghabhara, 512
event: The Ashoka legend cycle (84,000 stupas, Upagupta frame, gift-of-dirt prophecy) exists in Chinese translation by c. 306 CE - a TAQ for the legend stratum as formed literature; the cycle's internal frame places Ashoka ~100 years after the parinirvana (the short interval)
firmness_reason: The translation and its attribution are consistent across the catalogues; An Faqin's exact working years are a floruit, not a colophon year
notes: Campaign 2 Build A1: bounds the Ashoka-legend stratum, not Ashoka. The short (100-year) nirvana interval rides in this cargo; the long (218-year) interval rides in the Samantapasadika (trans. 488). Neither interval is independent of its lineage.
references: Taisho no. 2042 (Ayuwang zhuan); Taisho no. 2043 (Ayuwang jing); Strong, The Legend of King Ashoka (1983); Mukhopadhyaya, The Asokavadana (1960); Campaign 2 BUDDHA.md A1

indian_entity: Samantapasadika (Buddhaghosa's Vinaya commentary; Ceylon chronicle arithmetic)
chinese_source: Samantapasadika (T.1462), translated by Sanghabhadra at Canton, 488 CE
event: Buddhaghosa's Theravada Vinaya commentary - the carrier of the Ceylon 218-year nirvana-to-Ashoka interval - is translated into Chinese in 488; its translator Sanghabhadra is the same monk who placed the 975th dot of the dotted record at Canton in 489 (Campaign 1 case 1)
firmness_reason: Translation date is catalogue/colophon record; the identity of the dotted record's Sanghabhadra with the translator is the standard reading
notes: Campaign 2 Build A1: the 218-year interval and the dotted record enter China through the same man in consecutive years - the dependence graded in Campaign 1 case 1 made biographical.
references: Taisho no. 1462; Fei Changfang, Lidai Sanbao Ji (597); Campaign CORRECTIONS.md case 1; Campaign 2 BUDDHA.md A1

indian_entity: Buddha's birth and parinirvana (Chinese traditional dating)
chinese_source: Fei Changfang, Lidai Sanbao Ji (T.2034), completed 597 CE
event: Fei's catalogue records several mutually inconsistent backward-counting scales for the Buddha's dates (death dates derivable as early as 1005 BCE) and its own imperial chronology opens with the Buddha's birth in 687 BCE (King Zhuang of Zhou, jiawu year); the rival Zhao/Mu scheme (birth c. 1027 BCE in King Zhao's reign, death c. 949 BCE in King Mu's 52nd year) circulated via the lost Zhou Shu Yiji cited in court debate
firmness_reason: Firm as a record of what the catalogue says; CONTESTED-to-excluded as evidence for the Buddha's dates - the schemes are Chinese constructions (mofa countdown arithmetic and huahu polemic), mutually inconsistent by up to ~350 years, and all centuries earlier than every Indian-side candidate
notes: Campaign 2 Build A2 verdict: CORRECTED in the reverse direction - carried in the tool precisely so the 'Chinese traditional date of the Buddha' cannot be cited as an independent witness.
references: Taisho no. 2034 (Lidai Sanbao Ji); Zanning, Da Song Seng Shi Lue (999); Campaign 2 BUDDHA.md A2

chinese_source: EXTERNAL epigraphic anchor (non-Chinese): Aihole prashasti of Pulakesin II, composed by Ravikirti, dated Saka 556
event: Ravikirti's prashasti, dated 634 CE, already names Kalidasa (with Bharavi) as a byword for poetic fame - Kalidasa is classical before 634; the same inscription claims Pulakesin II's victory over Harsha
firmness_reason: A dated royal inscription; the Saka-era conversion is standard and the Kalidasa/Bharavi reference is in the published text
notes: Campaign 2 Build C5: added because the campaign brief described this TAQ as 'already in the spine' - it was not in anchors.json (checked 2026-11-17). Flagged external on the Gondophares/Quilon precedent. Chinese-translation evidence for Kalidasa: none (no kavya in any Tang catalogue).
references: Aihole prashasti of Pulakesin II (Epigraphia Indica VI); Campaign 2 VIKRAMADITYA.md C5

indian_entity: Shendu / India (first Chinese notice; Shu-Shendu-Bactria trade)
chinese_source: Shiji ch. 123 (Account of Dayuan), preserving Zhang Qian's report to Emperor Wu
event: Zhang Qian reports Shendu (India) at second hand: in Daxia (Bactria) he saw Shu cloth and Qiong bamboo staffs and was told merchants bought them in Shendu, several thousand li southeast of Daxia, whose people ride elephants to war beside a great river. He never entered India. Shu goods were already reaching Bactria via India before any Han mission
date_raw: Zhang Qian returns to Chang'an, Yuanshuo 3 (126 BCE); mission dispatched 138 BCE
firmness_reason: The report is preserved in the Shiji with the mission's dated frame (138-126 BCE); its content about India is explicitly hearsay, and is graded as hearsay
notes: Campaign 2 case D1: the spine's founding record. It dates China's knowledge of India and the trade's existence by c. 128 BCE - and names no Indian king, place or event. Zero-king content sets the channel's pattern from its first page.
references: Shiji ch. 123 (Dayuan liezhuan); Yang Juping, The Relations Between China and India and the Opening of the Southern Silk Road During the Han Dynasty; Campaign 2 CORRECTIONS2.md case D1

indian_entity: Arunasa's usurpation and defeat (Harsha's succession crisis)
chinese_source: Jiu Tang shu / Xin Tang shu (Tianzhu account); Cefu Yuangui embassy records
event: Wang Xuance's second mission (dispatched 647) arrives to find Harsha dead and the usurper Arunasa on the throne; the mission is attacked; Wang escapes to Tibet, returns in 648 with 7,000 Nepalese horse and Tibetan troops, defeats Arunasa in a three-day battle, and brings him captive to Chang'an
firmness_reason: Annalistic embassy sequence dated at every step; no Indian source records the usurpation at all. The usurper's equation with an Indian 'Arjuna' is probable, not firm, and is graded separately in the case file
notes: Campaign 2 case D3: distinct from Campaign 1 case 8 (Harsha's death date). This record grades the succession event, which Indian history does not contain.
references: Jiu Tang shu, Tianzhu account; Xin Tang shu, Tianzhu account; Cefu Yuangui; Campaign 2 CORRECTIONS2.md case D3

chinese_source: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji (Maharashtra chapter); presented 646
event: Xuanzang visits Maharashtra and describes its reigning king (Pulakesin II, unnamed in the text): far-reaching in his plans, obeyed by his vassals - and records that Siladitya (Harsha), who had mustered the forces of the five Indies against him, could not subdue him
firmness_reason: Dated eyewitness residence; the king is identified as Pulakesin II from the Indian side (the Aihole prashasti's Harsha-victory claim, 634), so the corroboration attaches to the frame - an unconquered Deccan king c. 641 - at probable
notes: Campaign 2 case D4: the Chinese witness independently attests the substance of the Aihole claim (Harsha checked by the Deccan king) a few years after the inscription; neither source dates the defeat itself (standard dating c. 618-619 is Indian-side).
references: Da Tang Xiyu Ji, Maharashtra chapter; Aihole prashasti (634); Campaign 2 CORRECTIONS2.md case D4

chinese_source: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji (Kamarupa chapter) and his biography (Huili)
event: Xuanzang is invited to Kamarupa, resides about a month with King Bhaskaravarman, and is escorted by him to Harsha's Kannauj assembly (643) - a dated eyewitness floruit for the king
firmness_reason: Pilgrim eyewitness with a dated itinerary; the king is named in the record (unlike the Gupta case), so the synchronism is direct, graded probable only because the month-level dates are itinerary reconstructions
notes: Campaign 2 case D5, first half: against an Indian side whose Kamarupa records (Nidhanpur plates) carry no absolute date, the pilgrim's visit is a fixed point in the reign.
references: Da Tang Xiyu Ji, Kamarupa chapter; Huili, Life of Xuanzang; Campaign 2 CORRECTIONS2.md case D5

chinese_source: Tang records of the Wang Xuance campaign (Jiu/Xin Tang shu; Cefu Yuangui tradition)
event: After the 648 victory over Arunasa, Bhaskaravarman supplies Wang Xuance's force with cattle, horses and provisions (the Tang tradition gives 30,000 head of cattle) - the king still reigning and cooperative in 648; the same record complex preserves his request for a portrait of Laozi and a translation of the Daodejing
firmness_reason: Annalistic logistics record; the Laozi-image request is famous but rests on the same record complex, so both halves are graded probable
notes: Campaign 2 case D5, second half: with the 642-643 eyewitness, brackets Bhaskaravarman's attested floruit to 642-648 from two independent Chinese directions.
references: Jiu Tang shu / Xin Tang shu, Tianzhu and Kamarupa material; Cefu Yuangui; Campaign 2 CORRECTIONS2.md case D5

indian_entity: Narasimhavarman II, Pallava of Kanchi (embassy to Tang)
chinese_source: Tang court record (Cefu Yuangui), Kaiyuan 8
event: Embassy from the king of South India, transcribed Che-li-Na-lo-seng-kia pao-to-pa-mo (Sri Narasimha Potavarman = Narasimhavarman II, Pallava of Kanchi): he offers his elephants and cavalry against the Arabs (Ta-che) and Tibetans (T'ou-po), asks the emperor to name his army and a temple he has built for the emperor; Xuanzong names the army 'the army which cherished virtue' (Huai-de) and the temple Guihua si, and sends a return embassy conferring a brevet title on the king
firmness_reason: Court record with a reign-era date to the month; the name transcription is phonetically transparent and the identification with Narasimhavarman II is the standard reading (Sastri). The popular claim that the embassy was 'led by Vajrabodhi' is Sastri's inference and is NOT in the record
notes: Campaign 2 case D6: a named Pallava king on his throne in a dated Chinese court record, independently confirming the inscriptional reign bracket (c. 700-728). The temple named by the emperor is plausibly - not provably - the Nagapattinam vihara later called the China Pagoda.
references: Cefu Yuangui, Kaiyuan 8 entries; Sastri, The Colas / Foreign Notices of South India; Mahalingam, Readings in South Indian History; Campaign 2 CORRECTIONS2.md case D6

indian_entity: Mahabodhi Sangharama (Sinhalese monastery at Bodh Gaya; Meghavarna embassy tradition)
chinese_source: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji (Magadha / Mahabodhi chapter)
event: Xuanzang describes the great Sinhalese monastery north of the Bodhi tree (three storeys, six halls, over 1,000 Sthavira monks) standing in 637, and transmits its foundation tradition: a king of Ceylon sent gifts to the Indian emperor and obtained permission to build it for Sinhalese pilgrims. Neither king is named in his text
firmness_reason: The monastery's existence in 637 is eyewitness (firm as observation); the foundation story is received tradition recorded by the pilgrim, and the named pairing Meghavarna-Samudragupta is a scholarly join with the Allahabad prashasti's Simhala missions, not a statement of either source
notes: Campaign 2 case D7: bounds the monastery (standing by 637) and corroborates the event class (a Ceylon embassy obtained a Gupta emperor's building permission); it does not date Samudragupta, whose frame is the Gupta era's own.
references: Da Tang Xiyu Ji, Mahabodhi chapter; Allahabad pillar prashasti of Samudragupta; Campaign 2 CORRECTIONS2.md case D7

indian_entity: The six sramana teachers (Purana, Gosala, Ajita, Pakudha, Sanjaya, Nigantha Nataputta)
chinese_source: Dirghagama (T.1), sutra 27 (Shamenguo jing), read out by Buddhayasas, translated by Zhu Fonian, Chang'an; second recension in Yijing's Mulasarvavastivada Vinaya Sanghabhedavastu (T.1450), 710
event: The six sramana teachers - Purana Kassapa, Makkhali Gosala, Ajita Kesakambala, Pakudha Kaccayana, Sanjaya Belatthiputta, Nigantha Nataputta (Mahavira) - are preserved as a fixed list with fixed one-line doctrines in the Sramanyaphala-sutra as translated into Chinese in 413 CE: a TAQ for the six-teachers stratum as fossilised syllabus material
date_raw: Later Qin, Hongshi era (translation completed 413 CE)
firmness_reason: The Dirghagama translation date (412-413) is catalogue/colophon record; the bound applies to the textual stratum, not to the teachers' floruits, which rest on the Buddha-synchronism of tradition class
notes: Campaign 2 case E2: carried so the tool records the distinction this campaign insists on - China dates the list, not the men. Mahavira's own interval is chained to the Buddha result (MAHAVIRA.md E1), not derived from this record.
references: Taisho no. 1 (Dirghagama), sutra 27; Taisho no. 1450 (Sanghabhedavastu, trans. Yijing 710); Chinaknowledge, Chang ahan jing; Campaign 2 MAHAVIRA.md E2

chinese_source: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji (Pundravardhana and Samatata chapters; India taxonomy juan 2); record presented 646
event: Xuanzang counts the naked Nirgranthas (Jains) as the most numerous non-Buddhist sectaries at Pundravardhana and again at Samatata, and describes the order from observation (naked, hair-plucking, cracked skin) - a dated eyewitness snapshot of Jain communities thriving across Bengal eleven centuries after Mahavira
firmness_reason: Dated eyewitness observation, the spine's zero-lag class; graded probable because the pilgrim's 'most numerous' is an impression, not a census, and the Ni-kien = Nirgrantha = Jain identification, though standard, is an identification
notes: Campaign 2 case E3: pins the order's survival and distribution in the 7th century; says nothing about its origins. No anchor is offered for Mahavira himself, Parsva, Gosala or the Buddha's teachers - the Chinese record dates none of them (MAHAVIRA.md E1, E4-E6).
references: Da Tang Xiyu Ji, Pundravardhana / Samatata chapters; Beal, Si-yu-ki (Buddhist Records of the Western World); Banglapedia, Chinese Accounts; Campaign 2 MAHAVIRA.md E3

chinese_source: EXTERNAL Tibetan anchor: Tengyur, Toh 4310 (with Candranandana's commentary), translation of the later-diffusion (phyi dar) period
event: Vagbhata's Astangahrdaya — the one great medical samhita the Tibetan canon took — is translated into Tibetan in the translation enterprise associated with Rinchen Zangpo (958-1055)
date_raw: Later diffusion period, Rinchen Zangpo's lifetime
firmness_reason: The Tengyur inclusion is certain; the precise translation date and team rest on the colophon tradition of the phyi dar period
notes: The loosest of Vagbhata's three foreign brackets (Yijing 691 and the Firdaws 850 both bite earlier) — but the socially largest: this translation is why the Hrdaya, not Caraka or Susruta, became Tibet's Ayurveda.
references: Vogel, Vagbhata's Astangahrdayasamhita: the First Five Chapters of its Tibetan Version (1965); Bu ston, History of Buddhism (chos 'byung)

indian_entity: Early Ayurvedic formulary tradition (Navanitaka; Caraka/Susruta/Bhela-line material)
chinese_source: EXTERNAL physical anchor (non-Chinese record): birch-bark manuscript in Gupta script, excavated from a stupa near Kucha (Xinjiang), now Bodleian MS Sansk. c.17
event: Three of the Bower Manuscript's seven treatises are medical; the Navanitaka formulary opens with a recipe that also stands in the Caraka Samhita and excerpts Caraka-, Susruta- and Bhela-line material
date_raw: Palaeographic dating (Gupta script; letter ya forms); no radiocarbon published
firmness_reason: Palaeographic range (Sander 500-550; Callewaert c. 450; Hoernle's final view 4th-5th c.); a published radiocarbon date would make it firm
notes: A TAQ for the formulary SYSTEM behind the samhitas, not for any one samhita's final form: by c. 500 the eight-branch corpus was mature and excerptable on the Silk Road.
references: Hoernle (ed.), The Bower Manuscript (1893-1912); Lore Sander (1986), palaeographic analysis; Wujastyk, The Roots of Ayurveda (2003)

chinese_source: Da zhuangyan lun jing (Sutralankara, T.201), Chinese translation attributed to Kumarajiva's bureau, Chang'an
event: The Chinese Sutralankara tells of Kaniska's court attended by the minister Mathara, the bodhisattva Asvaghosa, the minister Devadharma and the physician Caraka — the earliest datable carrier of the tradition that Caraka was Kaniska's physician (identified by Sylvain Levi, 1896)
date_raw: Later Qin, Hongshi era (Kumarajiva's Chang'an translation activity)
firmness_reason: T.201's attribution to Kumarajiva is traditional catalogue evidence, and the passage dates the TRADITION, not the redactor: the story is attested ~250 years after the event it claims
notes: Combined with the Kaniska epoch bound (c. 125-165, Campaign Case 2), the tradition if granted puts the Caraka redaction layer in the mid-2nd c. CE. 'Caraka' may name a school or professional type; the identification is unprovable from this carrier alone.
references: Sylvain Levi, Journal Asiatique (1896), on the Sutralankara's Kaniska court; Encyclopaedia Iranica, s.v. Caraka; Meulenbeld, History of Indian Medical Literature IA (1999)

indian_entity: Organised charitable medicine in India (Pataliputra dispensaries)
chinese_source: Faxian, Foguo Ji (Record of Buddhist Kingdoms), Pataliputra chapter
event: Faxian, resident in Pataliputra, describes houses established by Vaisya elders for dispensing charity and medicine: the destitute and diseased attend, physicians examine them, and food and medicine are provided free
date_raw: Faxian's Indian sojourn; three years resident in Pataliputra
firmness_reason: A dated eyewitness describing what he saw in the city he lived in; the spine's standard pilgrim grade at its strongest
notes: An infrastructure anchor: dates no text, but proves institutional, physician-staffed charitable medicine in a major Indian city within Drdhabala's floruit window (300-500).
references: Faxian, Foguo Ji, tr. Legge (1886), ch. on Pataliputra; Campaign anchor faxian-gupta frame (Case 12)

indian_entity: Indian medical books in Arabic (Sharaka, Susrud, Ashtankar)
chinese_source: EXTERNAL Arabic anchor: Ibn al-Nadim, Kitab al-Fihrist, compiled 987-988, discourse on the ancient sciences
event: The Fihrist catalogues the Indian medical books available in Arabic — Sharaka (Caraka), Susrud (Susruta, tr. Mankha), the Nidana, a book on poisons by Shanaq, and the Ashtankar — most plausibly Vagbhata's Astanga work in Arabic dress
firmness_reason: A dated catalogue of books its compiler handled; the Ashtankar identification is the one debated element and is corroborative only, the Firdaws (850) attestation of the Hrdaya being earlier and firmer
notes: The bibliographic terminus of the Barmakid translation movement: by 987 the Ayurvedic canon was a catalogued section of Arabic medicine.
references: Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist, tr. Dodge (1970); Ullmann, Islamic Medicine (1978)

indian_entity: The Ayurvedic canon in Arabic (Caraka, Susruta, Madhavanidana, Astangahrdaya)
chinese_source: EXTERNAL Arabic anchor: Ali ibn Rabban al-Tabari, Firdaws al-Hikma (Paradise of Wisdom), completed c. 850, part VII
event: Al-Tabari closes his medical encyclopedia with a 36-chapter summary of Indian medicine drawn from four named books: Charaka (Jarak), Susruta (Susrud), the Nidana (Niddin = Madhavakara's Rugviniscaya) and the Astangahrdaya (Ashtanqahrada)
date_raw: Composed at the court of al-Mutawakil, c. 849-850
firmness_reason: A dated, extant work; Meyerhof's identification of the four Arabic titles with the four Sanskrit works is the standard reading (Isis 16, 1931; Siggel's 1951 edition of the Indian chapters)
notes: One dated page brackets four canon texts at once: Caraka, Susruta, Madhava (c. 700) and Vagbhata's Hrdaya all existed in Arabic-accessible form by 850. The earliest datable Arabic attestation of Caraka's content.
references: Meyerhof, Isis 16.1 (1931); Siggel, Die indischen Bucher aus dem Paradies der Weisheit (1951)

indian_entity: Indian oculist practising in China (golden-scalpel cataract couching)
chinese_source: Liu Yuxi (772-842), poem 'Presented to the Brahmin Monk Eye-Doctor' (Zeng yanyi poluomen seng), with the companion reply poem of winter 837
event: Liu Yuxi, himself medically literate, addresses the Indian Brahmin monk whose golden-scalpel art is to lift his three years of blindness; a dated companion poem of winter 837 celebrates the cure — 'the golden scalpel is no longer needed'
date_raw: Tang, Kaicheng 2 winter (837) for the cure poem
firmness_reason: The poems are datable only through Liu Yuxi's biography and Pei Du's Luoyang tenure; the 837 companion poem anchors the cure, the address poem itself may be slightly earlier
notes: The signature operation of the Susruta tradition, performed on a named, datable Chinese patient in the 830s — the transmission at the level of the individual practitioner's hands.
references: Quan Tang Shi, Liu Yuxi poems; Religions 14:880 (2023), on Tang Buddhist ophthalmology

indian_entity: Indian physician at the Tang court (Narayanasvamin's longevity drug)
chinese_source: Jiu Tang Shu (Tianzhu account) and Zizhi Tongjian, s.a. 648-649
event: Wang Xuance's returning mission brings the Magadhan brahmin Narayanasvamin to Chang'an; under Taizong's patronage he compounds a longevity drug — the emperor dies in 649, and the annalists leave the elixir beside the death
firmness_reason: Annalistic record of a named foreign specialist at court; the elixir episode is told with a moralising edge, so the fact of the commission is firmer than its pharmacology
notes: Dates Indian medicine's prestige at the Tang throne, not any text. Gaozong's reign adds the East Indian monk-physician Lokaditya, sent to gather drugs from the southern seas.
references: Jiu Tang Shu, juan 198 (Tianzhu); Zizhi Tongjian, juan 199

indian_entity: Indian formulary material in China (Jivaka prescriptions; Brahmin massage method)
chinese_source: Sun Simiao, Beiji Qianjin Yaofang (Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold), completed 652
event: Sun Simiao's dated formulary incorporates Indian material under Indian names: formulas attributed to Jivaka (incl. the Jivaka myriad-disease pill), a Jivaka saying traced to Caraka Samhita Sutrasthana 26.12 ('nothing in the world is not a medicine'), and the 'Brahmin method' of massage with the eighteen postures of Tianzhu
firmness_reason: A dated, extant Chinese compilation citing its Indian material by name; the Caraka line arrives under Jivaka's attribution, which is why the record is firm for Indian formulary circulation and only indirect for Caraka's text
notes: The eastward channel in one record: Ayurveda reached China as attributed formulas and body practices inside Chinese books, not as translated samhitas.
references: Deshpande, Indian J. Hist. Sci. 43.2 (2008); Unschuld, Medicine in China: A History of Pharmaceutics (1986)

indian_entity: Indian medical literature in Chinese translation (Brahmin pharmacopoeias, Nagarjuna pharmacopoeia, Jivaka formulas)
chinese_source: Sui shu, Jingji zhi (bibliographic treatise), medical section
event: The Sui imperial bibliography lists eleven Indian medical titles in Chinese dress, incl. Pharmacopeia of the Brahmin Rsis (20 juan), Brahmin Pharmacopeia (5 juan), Pharmacopeia of Nagarjuna Bodhisattva (4 juan), Essential Formulas of Famous Physicians of the Western Regions (4 juan), Jivaka's Formulas (2 juan) — most inherited from the Liang imperial catalogue
firmness_reason: A dated imperial catalogue entry is the spine's standard firm existence proof; the titles themselves are lost, so it dates a transmission, not contents
notes: What it does NOT list matters equally: no Caraka and no Susruta translation is recorded here or in any Chinese bibliography — the great samhitas never entered China as books. The Nagarjuna of the pharmacopoeia is the medical/alchemical namesake, not evidence about the Madhyamika.
references: Sui shu, juan 34 (Jingji zhi 3); Deshpande, 'Glimpses of Ayurveda in Medieval Chinese Medicine', Indian J. Hist. Sci. 43.2 (2008)

chinese_source: EXTERNAL Arabic anchor: Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist (987), on the Barmakid translation movement
event: The Fihrist records that Mankha (Manka), an Indian physician at the Abbasid court, translated Susruta from Sanskrit into Arabic for the vizier Yahya ibn Khalid al-Barmaki
date_raw: Yahya ibn Khalid's vizierate under Harun al-Rashid, ended by the Barmakid fall
firmness_reason: The translation is recorded in a dated catalogue two centuries later; Mankha's presence at Harun's court is independently remembered (he is said to have cured the caliph), but no colophon of the translation itself survives
notes: Susruta existed, complete enough to translate whole, by 803 at the latest — three centuries after the internal evidence closes its present form. A confirmation anchor, not a tightening one.
references: Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist, tr. Dodge (1970), chapter on Indian medicine; Ibn Abi Usaybi'a, Uyun al-anba; Ullmann, Islamic Medicine (1978)

indian_entity: Susruta Samhita, complete six-book text (oldest dated manuscript)
chinese_source: EXTERNAL physical anchor (non-Chinese record): palm-leaf manuscript, Kaiser Library, Kathmandu, MS KL 699
event: The oldest surviving manuscript of the Susruta Samhita, dated by its colophon era to 878 CE, already contains the complete text including the Uttaratantra
firmness_reason: The 878 date rests on the reading of the manuscript's colophon era; the manuscript's completeness is directly inspectable
notes: A physical TAQ for the FINISHED Susruta: whatever the layers' dates, the six-book whole existed in this form by 878 — comfortably after the internal c. 500 closure and before Dalhana's commentary (c. 1200).
references: Wujastyk, The Roots of Ayurveda (2003); Meulenbeld, HIML IA (1999), on the Susruta manuscript tradition

indian_entity: Indian ophthalmology and Jivaka formulary in China (Tianzhu eye treatise; golden-scalpel couching)
chinese_source: Wang Tao, Waitai Miyao (Secret Essentials of an Official), completed 752, juan 21 (eye diseases) and passim
event: Wang Tao's dated formulary (6,900 prescriptions, sources named) carries Jivaka-attributed remedies throughout, and its eye section opens with the Preface to the Indian (Tianzhu) Treatise on Eyes by Master Xie of Longshang, who received the doctrine from a Western monk — followed by the first detailed Chinese account of golden-scalpel cataract couching
firmness_reason: A dated, extant compilation that names its sources; the Indian provenance of the eye treatise is stated by its Chinese transmitter himself
notes: Indian ophthalmology existed as a TEXT in China by 752. A large share of all Indian-derived prescriptions preserved in Chinese literature is concentrated in this one book (Fan's count).
references: Waitai Miyao, juan 21; Fan Ka Wai, and Deshpande, Indian J. Hist. Sci. 43.2 (2008); Religions 14:880 (2023), on Tang Buddhist ophthalmology

indian_entity: Indian ('Brahmin') prescription in the Tang imperial pharmacopoeia
chinese_source: Su Jing et al., Xinxiu Bencao (Newly Revised Materia Medica), imperial commission, 659
event: The Tang state pharmacopoeia records a 'Brahmin's prescription' as the known remedy for beriberi (jiaoqi), in all probability carried to China by an Indian Buddhist monk
firmness_reason: A dated imperial pharmacopoeia entry; the Indian provenance is stated in the record itself
notes: An Indian formula with official Chinese status by 659 — the transmission at the level of practice, a generation before Yijing's eyewitness account of the system behind it.
references: Xinxiu Bencao (659), beriberi entries; Deshpande, Indian J. Hist. Sci. 43.2 (2008)

indian_entity: Cikitsavidya (medicine) as a formal Indian science
chinese_source: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji (646), juan 2, on Indian education
event: Xuanzang lists the five sciences of the standard Indian curriculum — grammar, crafts, cikitsavidya (the science of medicine), logic and inner science — taught to students across India
firmness_reason: Dated eyewitness synthesis by the pilgrim who had just spent over a decade studying in India
notes: Attests medicine's institutional status — a named, teachable sastra — in mid-7th-century India, independent of any single text's date.
references: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji, juan 2; tr. Beal, Buddhist Records of the Western World (1884)

indian_entity: Vagbhata's Astanga synthesis (the eight branches epitomised in one work)
chinese_source: Yijing, Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan (written 691), vol. 3, sections 27-29 (on the origin of disease, on medicine, on harmful drugs)
event: Yijing, resident in India 673-685, names the eight branches of Indian medicine and reports that they 'formerly existed in eight books, but lately a man has compiled them into one fascicle' — the standard scholarly identification of the unnamed epitome is Vagbhata's Astanga synthesis
firmness_reason: Yijing's text and date are firm and he is a resident eyewitness; the one inferential step is identifying his anonymous 'one fascicle' epitome with Vagbhata's Astanga works (the reading standard since Takakusu)
notes: The sharpest foreign bracket on Vagbhata anywhere: the synthesis existed by 691 and was recent enough to remark on — pressing the c. 600-650 window from above. Yijing's sections 27-29 are also the fullest dated foreign description of Indian medicine as practised.
references: Yijing, Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan, tr. Takakusu (1896), chs. 27-29 and note; J. Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine 20:92 (2024), analysis of the medical chapters
